Neonates of the Western jumping mouse (Zapus princeps) weigh approximately 0.8 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.8 grams] at parturition, a value derived from comparative data on the closely related meadow jumping mouse (Zapus hudsonius). This modest birth mass, typical of altricial rodents, is followed by a period of rapid growth within the nest. The mothers, which are relatively small for a hibernating rodent, reach an ultimate wet weight for females of 35 grams [Wwi = 35 grams] according to field records, although body mass can vary between 17 and 40 grams depending on season and reproductive status. Under laboratory conditions maintained at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the gestation time is approximately 19 days [tg = approximately 19 days], a duration that is somewhat shorter than that of many similarly sized cricetid rodents and likely reflects the energetic constraints imposed by a short active season in montane habitats. The altricial neonates are entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial postnatal period, and their low birth weight underscores the substantial proportional investment required by the mother to bring each litter to term.

The developmental trajectory of Zapus princeps proceeds through several well-defined milestones following birth. Under controlled conditions maintained at 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], the time since birth at weaning is 30 days [tx = 30 days] and the time since birth at puberty, which marks the onset of gametogenesis and reproductive activation, is estimated at 61 days [tp = 61 days]. During this suckling stage, the nursing offspring are completely dependent on milk obtained from the lactating female. After the dietary transition to solid food is complete, the young continue to grow and develop rapidly. These values, based on studies of the congener Zapus hudsonius, suggest that individuals born early in the summer breeding season can achieve sexual maturity within the same active period, allowing them to potentially reproduce in the year of their birth before entering hibernation in the autumn. The relatively rapid maturation is an important life-history adaptation to the short growing season characteristic of its high-altitude and northern range.

Reproductive output in the Western jumping mouse is modest but consistent with its life-history strategy. Females typically produce a single litter per year [F_R_i = single litter per year], with each litter containing 4 to 8 pups [N_R_i = each litter containing 4 to 8 pups]. This maximum reproductive rate reflects the energetic challenges of raising altricial young in a brief alpine summer, where the availability of seeds and arthropod prey is temporally constrained. Field surveys and captive breeding records, maintained at a baseline temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C], confirm this pattern of a single annual reproductive event. The combination of relatively small litter sizes and a solitary annual breeding effort places Zapus princeps at the slow end of the reproductive spectrum among small-bodied rodents, a strategy that is likely linked to its dependence on fat accumulation for successful hibernation. The pups, born in a subniveal nest lined with dried grasses, are weaned after completing the 30-day suckling period and must rapidly gain sufficient mass to survive their first winter torpor.

Physiological measurements provide further insight into the metabolic demands placed on this species. Basal oxygen consumption, or the maximum basal metabolic rate (BMR), was recorded at 56.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 56.6 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at a thermoneutral body temperature of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. This level of resting metabolism is typical for a mammal of its size and reflects the heightened energetic costs associated with endothermy in a small body. The relatively high mass-specific metabolic rate is necessary to sustain the elevated body temperature required for activity and digestion during the brief growing season. This physiological trait also has implications for the species' ecology, as it necessitates a high rate of daily food intake, primarily consisting of seeds, berries, and insects. The need to maintain this metabolic rate while also depositing sufficient fat reserves for hibernation creates a tight energetic budget, particularly for lactating females who must simultaneously support their growing offspring in the weeks before autumn.

Maximum lifespan in the wild for Zapus princeps is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years], though this estimate is based on records obtained under the standard thermal conditions of 35.6 °C [T = 35.6 °C]. In the harsh alpine and subalpine meadows it inhabits across the Rocky Mountains and other western ranges, most individuals likely succumb to predation, starvation, or the energetic costs of failed hibernation long before reaching this upper limit. Interestingly, this lifespan is relatively long for a mouse of its size, a fact that is consistent with its slow life-history pace, featuring a single annual litter. The post-reproductive mortality experienced by older individuals typically results from senescence-related physiological decline following the final breeding season. The relatively short active season, combined with the lengthy period of winter torpor, imposes a strong selective pressure for efficient energy use, and the species' life-history parameters — from low birth weight to modest adult mass and a solitary yearly reproductive bout — appear tightly coadapted to this challenging environment.
